questions.q: What specifically causes Git to report a merge conflict?
options: Both branches changing the exact same lines of the exact same file in different ways
Any two branches being merged at all, every time
The repository running out of disk space
Merging a branch that has no commits
questions.explain: Git can combine most changes automatically; it only stops when it can't guess which of two conflicting edits to the same lines you want.

questions.q: In a conflict marker block, what does the section between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` represent?
options: A random Git error message
The version of those lines from the branch you're currently on
The version from the branch being merged in
A permanently deleted section of the file
questions.explain: HEAD marks the content from your current branch; the section after ======= is from the branch being merged in.

questions.q: What does running `git add` on a previously conflicted file tell Git?
options: To delete the file entirely
To undo the merge completely
Nothing — add has no special meaning during a conflict
That this file's conflict is now resolved and ready to be included in the merge commit
questions.explain: Staging a conflicted file after editing it is exactly how you tell Git the conflict in that file has been resolved.

questions.q: What does GitHub's web-based conflict editor let you do, as shown on a pull request that can't merge automatically?
options: Automatically delete one of the two branches
Nothing — conflicts on GitHub can only ever be resolved locally
Edit the conflicting file directly in the browser, with the same markers, then mark it resolved and commit the merge
Force-push over the conflict without resolving it
questions.explain: GitHub's conflict editor mirrors the local experience — same markers, editable in the browser, with buttons to mark resolved and commit the merge.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is resolving a conflict locally in your own editor usually the better choice over GitHub's browser editor?
options: Always — the browser editor should never be used
For anything nontrivial, where running the code and seeing surrounding context actually matters
Only when working alone with no collaborators
Never — the browser editor is always superior
questions.explain: The browser editor is handy for small, simple conflicts, but local resolution gives you the full context and ability to actually run the code.
